evidence.field: Discussion of oracle-bone uses of 工 and 百工, especially lines 244–308
evidence.text: The author reviews contrasting readings of oracle-bone 工 as official/官 and argues that the occurrences show differing social positions; examples include 丧工, 执工, 多工, and 百工. He cautions against treating every oracle-bone use as simply an official title and interprets some 多工/百工 uses as makers of fine handicrafts. He also notes that Zhou 百工 contexts vary in institutional status. This supports retaining distinctions among title/status and craft-worker uses rather than merging them into one sense.
evidence.title: 商代“宗工”名称考

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, Taiwan Ministry of Education, 2024 version 7
evidence.field: 工 entry, modern and historical definition sections, lines 54–78
evidence.text: The dictionary lists senses for 工 including refined/skillful, skilled worker, official, musician, skill, being skilled, laboring activity, construction, industrial abbreviation, and a verb/nominal equivalent of 功. It supplies both classical quotations and unmarked modern examples such as 木工、矿工、水電工 for the worker sense and 工整 for refined/skillful. The entry does not mark these current examples obsolete, supporting present usage for those senses while leaving their semantic chronology unresolved.

gaps: The graph's exact depicted object remains disputed: the inspected paleographic database reports a bladed tool with possible square function, a square interpretation, and a building-tool proposal. No inspected primary artifact image or specialist publication resolved the identification.

No independently recoverable name or pronunciation for the proposed depicted tool was found. The character's own reconstructed pronunciation (*kˤoŋ in Baxter–Sagart; *koːŋ in Zhengzhang) cannot establish the object's name; the tool-pictograph account does not require a sound loan, so an object-name match is not established or needed here.

The opened paleographic entry lists oracle-bone and bronze artifact identifiers but does not date them; an earliest dated attestation for each sense (tool, place/state name, official/status, craft worker, work, achievement, and 貢 loan) remains unverified.

The semantic path from a tool graph to skilled work, worker, work/labor, skill, and achievement is not established as one chronological chain by the inspected sources. Shuowen's 巧飾 account and the modern paleographic tool analysis conflict in their accounts of the graph's original meaning.

The early official/status use and later craft/work uses should not be collapsed. The sources inspected do not establish whether they are semantically related, homonymous, or reflect graphic loan in all contexts.

The reported 工(貢) examples are whole-graph loans for 貢, distinct from 工 serving as a phonetic component in derived characters. Their exact dates and the phonological basis at the time of borrowing were not established.

工, 功, and 攻 have close readings in the cited reconstruction tables, but no independently inspected primary source established the dossier's proposed semantic etymologies connecting their word senses. A shared or similar reconstructed sound alone does not prove that etymology.

No sound component occurs inside 工 itself, so there is no component pronunciation/origin relation to classify for this character. The distinct shape 彡 in the Shuowen-reported ancient form 𢒄 is explicitly described there as part of that alternate graph, but the inspected sources do not establish it as an ancestor of 工.
The imported dossier's Burmese and Old Mon comparisons and the claim that 工 is an Austroasiatic area word were not independently verified in this research.

Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese readings are present in the dossier, but their dated transmission histories and earliest attestations were not investigated; Chinese spelling readings alone cannot establish a Japanese-origin account.

The precise object depicted by the early 工 graph remains disputed: the inspected paleographic source records a bladed tool with a possible square function, a square interpretation, and a building-tool interpretation.

The proposed graph-as-tool account does not establish the spoken name or pronunciation of the depicted object. 工’s reconstructed pronunciation cannot independently identify that object’s name; no separate name evidence was found.

The CUHK entry lists artifact identifiers but does not date each one in its displayed text. The earliest dated attestation for the tool graph, place or state name, official/status sense, craft occupation, work, achievement, and 貢 loan remains unverified.
The semantic route from proposed tool image to craft, worker, work, skill, and achievement is not established as one chronology. Shuowen’s 巧飾 explanation differs from the modern tool analysis.

The reported 工(貢) forms are whole-graph loans, separate from any sound-component analysis; no early borrowing pronunciation comparison or independently established 貢 sound evidence was found in the inspected pages.

工 has no internal sound component to classify. Shuowen’s 𢒄 is recorded as an alternate ancient graph with 彡, but the inspected sources do not establish whether it is an ancestor, variant, or other relation to 工.

The official Xiaoxuetang 工 query did not yield inspectable individual candidate labels or image URLs in the browser tool. The CUHK-linked image endpoints likewise lacked inspectable provenance. Thus no image candidate met the identity and reuse-provenance threshold.

The Commons page for the supplied candidate Shuowen Seal Radical 147.svg did not load, and the exact Commons imageinfo API URL was inaccessible. Unlike 工-seal.svg, no external character identity, original URL, or reuse terms could be verified for that candidate; do not select it from the local file alone.

Browser attempts to fetch original SVGs and thumbnails failed or returned no inspectable image block. File-page metadata and source links support the labeled vector illustrations, but direct pixel inspection was not completed in this interface.

The precise ancient object represented by 工 remains disputed. The inspected paleographic source reports blade/tool, square, and building-tool interpretations; no inspected primary artifact photograph or independently published specialist analysis resolved the disagreement.

The proposed tool’s original spoken name and pronunciation are not independently recoverable from the inspected evidence. 工’s reconstructed pronunciation cannot be used to infer the name of the depicted object.

The CUHK entry supplies inscription identifiers but no dates for those individual examples. Earliest dated attestation of the graph and of place-name, status/title, craft-worker, work, achievement, and 貢-loan uses remains undetermined here.

The path from a possible tool depiction to craft, occupation, work, skill, and achievement is not securely established. The Shuowen semantic explanation differs from the modern paleographic interpretations, and gloss lists alone cannot supply chronology.

工(貢) is reported as a whole-graph loan, not an internal sound-component analysis. The sound relation at the time of borrowing and the independent historical reading of 貢 were not verified in this pass.
The relationship between Shuowen’s 𢒄 and 工 is not classified by direction in the inspected source; do not assert an ancestor-to-descendant relation merely because the entry calls 𢒄 an ancient form.
The required official Unihan character-specific page did not expose an inspectable kMandarin row; current reading is available only from the supplied local row and other inspected secondary material.

Direct image pixels could not be inspected: Commons SVG requests returned unsupported-content errors and the bronze thumbnail returned a cache miss. The candidates are supported by their exact Commons file descriptions and source links, but should be visually checked by the separate image-review stage.

The historical candidates are modern vector redrawings of labeled script forms, not artifact photographs; they do not independently resolve the disputed object represented by 工. The paleographic entry retains competing tool/square interpretations.

No inspected source dates each cited artifact or establishes the first occurrence of each use. Keep the early oracle-bone, bronze, and transmitted-text examples distinct from claims about earliest attestation.

The proposed early referent remains disputed among tool, square and building-tool analyses. Shuowen's 巧飾 / 規榘 account is a separate historical interpretation; this evidence does not settle one origin account.

The relationship between tool-image proposals, craft/work senses, and official/status uses is not established as one chronology. The Southwest University article explicitly cautions against collapsing the different oracle-bone social uses into one official sense.
